title: Whatever is lovely (Philippians 4:8–9)
hook: whatever is true, noble, pure, lovely: think on these things

segments.voice: Yesterday, rejoice always, and your line was the peace that passes understanding. Which worry did you bring with a thank-you beside it? Day six hundred sixty-seven.

Scroll for ten minutes and count what went into your head. An argument between strangers. A crime two states away. Someone's perfect kitchen. An ad that knew what you'd been thinking about. None of it was chosen, exactly. It just arrived, and it stayed. The mind is like a kitchen: what you stock it with is what you end up cooking. Paul has just promised the Philippians a peace that will guard their hearts and minds. Now he tells them what to let through the gate. He gives them a list.

Here it is in the King James Bible, and it's worth hearing slowly: "Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things." Six whatsoevers, then two ifs. True. Honest, which in the old English means honorable, worthy of respect. Just. Pure. Lovely. Of good report, things that speak well. The word for lovely is a rare one. As far as we know, it appears nowhere else in the New Testament. It means pleasing, winsome, the kind of thing that makes you want to come closer. And here's a surprise. Several words on the list, virtue especially, come straight from the Greek moral philosophers of the day. Paul is borrowing the vocabulary that thoughtful people in a Greek city already used about the good life. He seems to be saying: whatever is genuinely good, wherever you find it, take it in. Then the verb: think on these things. The Greek word means to reckon, to count up, to dwell on deliberately. It's the same verb Paul used a few verses back, when he said he didn't count himself to have arrived. This isn't wishful thinking or ignoring what's wrong. It's choosing what you keep turning over. And he doesn't leave it as thinking. The next line: "Those things, which ye have both learned, and received, and heard, and seen in me, do: and the God of peace shall be with you." Think on them. Then do them. Yesterday it was the peace of God. Today, the God of peace.

Here's the practice: think about one lovely thing. Settle, and breathe. Pick one thing from the last few days that was true, or good, or simply lovely. A child's laugh. Light on a wall. Someone keeping a promise. A song. Not a big thing. Now stay with it on purpose. Recall the details: where you were, the sound, the color, the feeling. When your mind tries to drift back to a worry, notice, and bring it gently back to the lovely thing. That is the whole practice. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. The bell holds the time.
Whatever is lovely. Paul's list of what to let into the mind: true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, of good report.
Your line: think on these things. Today, before you open a feed, ask the six questions once. Is it true? Is it lovely? Then decide what gets in. Day six hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Many Christians memorize Philippians 4:8 and use it as a test for what they read, watch and talk about, and teachers and parents often post it in classrooms and homes.

fork.setup: your mind keeps returning to an argument you saw online. using Paul's list, what do you do?
options: keep replaying it so you're ready to win next time.
choose something true and lovely and dwell on that instead.
fork.reveal: "whatsoever things are lovely... think on these things." not denial: a deliberate choice of what to keep turning over.

original.note: Greek: lovely, pleasing, winsome. it is built on phil-, the root of friendly love.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice verse for a greeting card.
what it means: a deliberate list of what to let into the mind, then a call to do what you've learned.
what a scholar hears: logizesthe, reckon or count, the verb Paul used in 3:13 for not counting himself arrived, and a list borrowing the language of Greek moral philosophy.

notes: προσφιλής (4:8) is generally listed as occurring only here in the New Testament; the script hedges with 'as far as we know'. Confirm.
ἀρετή (virtue) appears in Paul's letters only here; the link to Greek moral philosophy is standard commentary. Confirm.
λογίζεσθε (4:8): the script links it to λογίζομαι in 3:13 ('I count not myself to have apprehended'). Confirm.
